transcript.text: Hi! Could you pull which customers spent less this quarter than last quarter? I'm thinking of sending them something to bring them back, maybe a 15% coupon. The sales export is attached. [shares sales.csv]

Thanks, I get it: you want the customers whose spend dropped from last quarter to this one, so you can send them a win-back offer like a 15% coupon. Your table has paid, cancelled and refunded orders. Should cancelled and refunded orders count toward "spent", or only paid ones? And is this a one-off list, or something you'd want to rerun each quarter?

Good questions, thanks. Only paid orders should count as spend. Cancelled and refunded orders aren't real revenue, so I'd exclude them, though I'd like to see how many there are first in case refunds are large for some customers. It's not a one-off. I'd rerun it each quarter, but this first list is for a campaign that goes out on the 15th next month.

I should also clarify the goal. Spending less this quarter than last isn't quite what I need. I want customers who are starting to lapse and who wouldn't buy again without a nudge. People whose spend just dipped may be buying on their normal schedule, and giving them coupons would waste them. So I'd like a way to rank customers by how likely they are to stop buying, and send the 1,000 coupons to the ones where the offer is most likely to change what they do.

The table has order_date, customer_id, amount, status, channel, region, and product_category. I'm comfortable with pivot tables and SQL-style logic but I haven't built a model. Is a simple scoring approach enough, like recency, frequency and spend trends? Or would you want to try a propensity model? My manager has to approve the final list, so I need something clear enough to explain in a few sentences.

A simple score is a good place to start, and it's easier to defend to your manager. A model is the heavier option. On refunds: of the 2,020 orders, 1,733 are paid, 188 are refunded and 99 are cancelled. Refunds touch 174 customers, so they're spread out, not concentrated. Two caveats:
- Only 938 customers have a paid order. Your 1,000 coupons would cover nearly everyone, so the ranking matters less than you might expect. - The table has no record of past coupons. Neither option can tell you who the offer would change. Both rank who is drifting away. Which option would you like?

choices.title: Transparent lapse score
choices.what: Using paid orders only, score each customer on recency, frequency and spend change from last quarter to this one, then rank them. Cancelled and refunded counts shown alongside. You get: A ranked list you can explain in three sentences to your manager, rerunnable each quarter. Trade-off: Ranks who is drifting away, not who the coupon would change. Weights are judgment calls, not learned. Effort: Quick, no modelling.

choices.title: Lapse propensity model
choices.what: Train a model on past customer behaviour to predict who stops buying, using paid orders only, and rank customers by that probability. You get: A data-driven risk ranking with an honest accuracy check on held-out customers. Trade-off: The table is modest in size, the result is harder to explain, and like the score it can't show who responds to a coupon. Effort: Longer, needs a clear definition of lapsed.

I'd also like the lapse cutoff stated clearly, for example 'no paid order in the last 90 days, but at least 3 paid orders in the prior 12 months.' Then I can check whether the cutoff makes sense against the calendar, since the campaign goes out on the 15th and I'll need to rerun it each quarter.

Good choice. DCLab is now building the lapse score from paid orders only. It will rank each customer on three things: how long since their last paid order, how often they buy, and whether their spend is trending down. Each customer will also get a plain-language reason, for example how long it has been since their last order compared with how often they usually buy. That should be easy to explain to your manager. You'll get a ranked list you can rerun each quarter, plus the refund and cancellation counts by customer. The score shows who is drifting away. It can't show who the coupon would change, because the table has no coupon history.

transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline, and show your 3% base rate next to it. **Why:** When positives are this rare, ROC-AUC can look strong even when many of the customers you flag aren't churners. Its false-positive rate divides by the huge pool of non-churners, so a lot of false alarms barely move it. PR-AUC tracks precision, which is what your retention team will feel. A random model's PR-AUC equals the base rate, so any lift over 3% is easy to read. **For your manager:** Add one plain number, such as "of the top slice of customers we flag, this share actually churn." Pick the slice to match how many customers your team can contact. Managers usually grasp that more easily than any AUC. Does that cover what you need?
Yes, that covers it. Give me one line I can paste on the slide.

Here's a line for the slide:

**"PR-AUC is our headline metric because only 3% of customers churn. A random model scores 3%, and ours scores [your PR-AUC], so it finds churners [X] times better than chance."**

Replace the two brackets with your own results. Good luck with the presentation.
